Background

This policy brief examines the spatial distribution and temporal trajectory of economic hardship across census tracts in Maricopa County, AZ. The analysis constructs a composite hardship index from three American Community Survey indicators — the poverty rate, the unemployment rate, and median household income (reverse-coded) — standardized and averaged into a single z-score measure. This index identifies neighborhoods where multiple dimensions of economic disadvantage overlap, providing a more nuanced picture than any single indicator alone.

The temporal analysis compares hardship levels in the 2009–2013 and 2015–2019 ACS 5-year windows, spanning the post-recession recovery decade. Using Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA), the analysis identifies statistically significant hot spots (clusters of high hardship) and cold spots (clusters of low hardship) at each time point, then classifies each tract’s trajectory — persistent, emerging, or dissolving — to reveal where hardship is entrenching, spreading, or receding. A three-point check using the 2012–2016 midpoint distinguishes monotonic trends from V-shaped or inverted-V patterns. If you selected a different county, review whether these temporal patterns match your local context.

Limitations

This analysis relies on ACS 5-year estimates, which carry margins of error that can be substantial at the census tract level. The temporal comparison (2013–2019) reflects the post-recession recovery decade and does not capture COVID-era disruptions. Most importantly: a declining hardship index in a tract may reflect genuine improvement for existing residents — or it may reflect displacement, with lower-income households replaced by higher-income newcomers. Census aggregate statistics cannot distinguish these processes. This analysis identifies candidate intervention areas; on-the-ground verification is essential before resource allocation decisions are made.
